title: Marcia's long grief
hook: Seneca writes to a mother still grieving her son after three years (Consolation to Marcia 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was receiving well: the gladness that pays the first installment. Your line was receive gladly.

There's a point after a death when people stop asking. The casseroles stop. The cards stop. Everyone else's calendar has moved on, and the person who lost someone is still standing in the same room. In Rome, a woman named Marcia had reached that point. Her son Metilius had died, and three years later, Seneca says, her grief was as fresh as the first day. So he wrote her a long letter.
screen: `WHEN PEOPLE STOP ASKING.` → `THREE YEARS LATER.` → `A LETTER TO MARCIA.`

segments.voice: First, who she was. Marcia's father was the historian Cremutius Cordus. Under the emperor Tiberius he was prosecuted over his history, which praised Brutus and Cassius, and he ended his own life rather than wait for the verdict. His books were ordered burned. Marcia helped save copies, and they came back into circulation. Seneca opens the letter by honoring that courage. He doesn't start by scolding. Second, he waited. He wouldn't have dared to argue with her grief in its first raw days, he says. He waited for time, the natural remedy, to do its work. What worried him, three years on, was that it hadn't: grief had become a habit, feeding itself, keeping her from life. Third, two mothers. Octavia, the sister of Augustus, lost her son Marcellus and grieved for the rest of her life. She wouldn't let anyone say his name. Livia, the wife of Augustus, lost her son Drusus and mourned him deeply. Then she let his name back into her life, and spoke of him often, gladly. Seneca asks Marcia which she wants to be like. His test isn't whether you still miss someone. It's whether you can bear to hear their name. Fourth, honesty about the letter. Some readers find parts of it too quick to argue with tears, and some parents who've lost a child would say some grief never fully leaves. Seneca's own letter shows something gentler, though. He let her grief have its time before he said a word.
screen: `CORDUS' DAUGHTER SAVED HIS BOOKS.` · `HE WAITED BEFORE HE SPOKE.` · `OCTAVIA AND LIVIA.` · `CAN YOU BEAR TO HEAR THE NAME?` · then, large: `GRIEF TAKES TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose loss is older than most people's patience: a friend whose parent died years ago, a neighbor whose husband is gone, maybe you. Don't try to fix anything; just sit with them in your mind for a while, and quietly say the name of the person they lost.
Luctus. Latin for mourning: Seneca wrote to a mother three years after her son died, and asked whether she could let his name back into her life. Today's word.
Your line: grief takes time. A name, said gently, can still be a gift. Day five hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca's consolations make a point of speaking the name of the person who died, long after others have stopped asking.

chat.says: My friend lost her mom years ago. Is it too late to mention her?
options: Grief takes time; asking about her mom by name, then mostly listening, can be kind.
Yes, after a year or so grief is over, so it's best never to bring it up.
No, just tell her it's been long enough and it's time to move on.
chat.meaning: Grief takes time, and some never fully leaves. Seneca's test was whether a loved name can be heard; asking gently, by name, honors that.

Marcia.meaning: a Roman mother whose son died; Seneca wrote to console her

Cremutius Cordus.meaning: Marcia's father, a historian whose books were ordered burned

Octavia.meaning: Augustus' sister, who grieved her son Marcellus all her life

Livia.meaning: Augustus' wife, who let her son Drusus' name back in

Tiberius.meaning: the Roman emperor when Cordus was prosecuted

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced superlative 'one of the oldest surviving consolations in Latin' (also from the trapdoor, now Tacitus's own remark on the burned books); fixed 'time was the first medicine, and he let it work' (Seneca says time, the natural remedy, had failed her); 'Seneca waited three years' overstated his timing; softened 'many people who've lost a child'; varied the 'Settle, and breathe' opener.
Marcia ch. 1: three years since the son's death, grief undiminished; Seneca says he would not have dared to oppose it in its first days; Marcia preserved her father's books. Confirm.

Cremutius Cordus: prosecuted in AD 25 for praising Brutus and calling Cassius 'the last of the Romans'; starved himself; books burned by decree of the senate, copies preserved (Tacitus, Annals 4.34–35). Confirm.
The son is named Metilius in the consolation; confirm.
Octavia (Marcellus) and Livia (Drusus) contrast is ch. 2–3; Areus the philosopher consoled Livia (ch. 4–5). Confirm.
'Among the earliest Latin consolations that survive whole' is hedged: Cicero's own Consolatio is lost. Confirm wording.
Job 2 (2026-10-07): Cordus' death now said as 'ended his own life' without the method (safe messaging); the fact is unchanged.
